label: Ephesians 1:5
text: "Predestinated" translates *proorizō* (προορίζω) — *horizō*, "to mark out a boundary" (our word "horizon" descends from the noun *horos*), prefixed by *pro*, "beforehand." It's a surveyor's word turned theological: God marked out the limits of our destiny before anything else was drawn on the map. The destination itself is named by *huiothesia*, "adoption," built from *tithēmi*, "to place," and *huios*, the word for a grown, legally-recognized son — not *teknon*, "a born child." Paul is borrowing the Roman legal custom in which an adopted son received full civil standing and inheritance rights regardless of birth. God does the birthing (we become *teknon*, born ones, at regeneration) and then, in the same predestining act, places us as *huios* — sons with legal standing to inherit. The agency clause, "through Jesus Christ," uses *dia* with the genitive, the preposition of the intermediate agent: Christ is the means by which the placement happens, not merely its occasion.
translation: He marked us out beforehand, with a view to our placement as adult sons for himself through Jesus Christ, according to what pleased his own desire.

label: Ephesians 1:6
text: "Freely bestowed" is *charitoō* (χαριτόω), built on the same root as *charis*, "grace" — the verb means, essentially, "to grace someone," to pursue and surround a person with favor. "The Beloved," naming Christ, is a perfect participle of *agapaō*: not "the one being loved" but "the one who has been loved and stands loved" — a settled, completed, permanent state rather than an ongoing feeling. Paul reaches for the perfect tense here because he wants the reader to hear the Father's love for the Son as a fixed fact, not a fluctuating sentiment. And the location matters grammatically as much as theologically: "in the Beloved" is a sphere within which grace operates — outside of Christ and his finished work, this grace has nowhere to land.
translation: To the praise of the glory of his grace, which he graced us with in the Beloved — the one who has been loved and stands loved.

label: Ephesians 1:7
text: "We have redemption" is present tense and durative — not "we got redemption once" but "we are continuously in possession of it," a standing state rather than a memory. Greek supplies three separate verbs for the idea of redemption, each catching a different frame: *agorazō*, "to buy in the marketplace" (the purchase itself); *exagorazō*, "to buy out of the market," implying the item is now permanently removed from sale; and *lutroō*, "to set free by paying a ransom." The noun Paul uses here, *apolutrōsis*, carries that last sense — release secured by a price paid, not a release granted out of leniency. "Forgiveness" is *aphesis*, from *aphiēmi*, "to send away" — sin is not excused but dispatched, sent off as if it had never been filed. And "trespasses" is *paraptōma*, literally "a fall to the side," the picture of a foot slipping off a path rather than of a target deliberately missed. The next verse describes the scale of this grace with *perisseuō*, "to super-abound, to exist in surplus beyond what was needed" — grace with excess built in, not grace rationed to just cover the debt.
translation: In whom we are continually having our redemption through his blood, the sending away of our trespasses, according to the wealth of his grace, which he made to super-abound toward us in every wisdom and understanding.

label: Ephesians 1:9
text: "Mystery" (*mustērion*) in Paul's vocabulary is not something baffling but something formerly sealed — a plan kept back and now disclosed, plain enough once opened. The "will" behind it is *thelēma*, desire rooted in the emotions, not *boulē*, a plan reasoned out by deliberation; God's disclosure of this plan flows out of his heart's affection, not a committee decision. "According to" is *kata*, a preposition whose root sense is "down over" — it describes something governing or pressing down on what follows. So the mystery isn't revealed arbitrarily; it's released under the governing hand of what pleased God (*eudokia*, "that which seemed good").
translation: Having made known to us the secret of his will, according to what pleased him, which he purposed within himself.

label: Ephesians 1:10
text: "Dispensation" translates *oikonomia* — *oikos*, "house," plus *nomos*, "law" or "management" — the word for running a household's affairs, not a theological era in itself but the administrative method applied to one. The "times" being administered are *kairoi*, not *chronoi*: Greek distinguishes ordinary ticking duration (*chronos*) from *kairos*, the decisive joint or hinge-point where one period gives way to the next. Paul is describing history's seams, not its minutes. "Gather together" is *anakephalaioō* — *ana*, "again," plus the root behind "head" or "sum" — picturing a return to a single head after fragmentation, the way a ledger's scattered entries get summed back to one total. Everything splintered by sin gets reheaded under Christ.
translation: With a view to an administration of the fullness of the seasons: to head up again the all things in the Christ — the things in the heavens and the things on the earth — in him.

label: Ephesians 1:11
text: The better manuscripts read not "we have obtained an inheritance" but "we were made an inheritance" — the saints are the thing possessed, God's own portion, rather than merely heirs receiving one. *Proorizō* returns from verse 5, the same surveyor's verb marking out boundaries in advance. And "counsel" here is *boulē*, deliberate, reasoned purpose, standing next to "will," *thelēma*, desire from the heart — Paul stacks both words to say God's choice is neither cold calculation alone nor impulse alone, but reasoned love and loving reason acting together.
translation: In whom also we were made a heritage, having been marked out beforehand according to the purpose of the one who works the all things according to the counsel of his will.

label: Ephesians 1:12
text: "Who first trusted" hides an unusual compound: *proelpizō*, "to hope beforehand" — not the ordinary verb for believing (*pisteuō*) but one built on *elpizō*, "to hope," with *pro* attached. It marks out Jewish believers specifically, those who held a Messianic hope in advance of the Messiah's actual coming — hoping ahead of the event that would confirm the hope. And "Christ" is simply the Greek transliteration of the word meaning "anointed one," the exact rendering of the Hebrew "Messiah" — two words, one title, carried across two languages into the one name we now use as though it were a surname.
translation: So that we should be to the praise of his glory — we who have hoped beforehand in the Christ.

label: Ephesians 1:13
text: "Sealed" is *sphragizō*, everyday commercial vocabulary — sealing a jar of produce for shipment, branding livestock, marking a finished transaction so no one tampers with it. Papyri from the period use the same verb for goods checked, certified, and closed off from further handling. Applied to the Holy Spirit, the image carries three ideas at once: a completed transaction (the price for sin has been paid, in full, no further negotiation), a mark of ownership (this belongs to someone now), and a guarantee of security (sealed goods travel safe). The Spirit himself is the seal — not a token he leaves behind, but his own presence taking up permanent residence.
translation: In whom you also, having heard the word of the truth, the good news of your salvation — in whom also having believed — you were sealed with the Spirit of the promise, the Holy Spirit.

label: Ephesians 1:14
text: "Earnest" is *arrabōn*, a term straight out of the marketplace — a deposit paid up front as a pledge that the rest is coming. Papyri receipts use the word for exactly this: a down payment on a cow, an advance to a mouse-catcher for pest control, money in hand guaranteeing a fuller payment later. Applied to the Spirit, the picture is that God has already handed over a first installment of the salvation he intends to complete — his indwelling presence now is the guarantee, not a bonus, of what's still owed. "Purchased possession" is *peripoiēsis*, the general idea of something acquired and kept for oneself — the saints as God's own preserved property, awaiting the final payment, which Paul elsewhere identifies with the resurrection of the body.
translation: Who is a down payment of our inheritance, until the redeeming of the possession being preserved, to the praise of his glory.

label: Ephesians 1:17
text: "Spirit" here has no definite article, and it's ambiguous by design: not simply the Holy Spirit as a separate gift, and not simply the human spirit, but the human spirit as it operates under the Holy Spirit's influence — a settled disposition of wisdom rather than a fresh possession, since the Ephesians already had the Spirit. Paul prays for that disposition to characterize them, not for something they lack. "Knowledge" is *epignōsis*, not the simple word for knowing (*gnōsis*) but the compound with *epi* attached, intensifying it toward full, precise, experiential acquaintance — knowledge that has arrived, not knowledge still gathering data.
translation: That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of the glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in full knowledge of him.

label: Ephesians 1:18
text:
"The eyes of your understanding" is literally "the eyes of your heart" — *kardia* in Greek covers not just emotion but the whole faculty of reasoning and perceiving, so Paul is praying for clarified thinking as much as clarified feeling. "Being enlightened" is a perfect participle: a completed past act whose light-filled result still stands, not a flickering illumination that needs relighting. The word for "what" (*tis*) matters too — Paul isn't asking that they grasp how great the hope is, but simply what it actually is, its content rather than its size.

The prayer's third request, spilling into the next two verses, piles up four separate Greek words for power: *dunamis*, inherent capacity; *energeia*, power actually at work; *kratos*, strength as displayed; *ischus*, power as a built-in endowment. Stacked together they describe not one attribute among many but power measured against power, the way you'd triangulate a distance from several fixed points. That power is identified concretely: it's the same force God put to work (*energeō*) raising Christ bodily out from among the dead and seating him at his right hand — resurrection power, already spent once, now aimed at believers.
translation: The eyes of your heart having been enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what is the wealth of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who are believing, measured by the operative strength of his might, which he put to work in the Christ when he raised him out from among the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenlies.

label: Ephesians 1:21
text:
Paul stacks four rank-words in a row — *archē*, "first one, ruler"; *exousia*, "delegated authority"; *dunamis*, "power"; *kuriotēs*, "lordship" — the standard Jewish vocabulary for tiers of angelic beings, good and fallen alike. "Far above" translates *huperanō*, a doubled-up preposition ("over" plus "above") that piles emphasis on emphasis, as if one "above" wasn't enough. "World" is *aiōn*, not *kosmos* — Paul means duration, an age with a beginning and end, not the created order itself; Christ outranks every power in this age and in the one still to come.

The chapter's close adds "put in subjection," *hupotassō*, military language for placing troops under a commanding officer — Christ's exaltation is a formal transfer of command, not a vague honor. "Church" is *ekklēsia*, "a called-out assembly." And "fulness," *plērōma*, is deliberately double-edged: the church is what Christ fills, and simultaneously that through which his fulness is expressed to the world — container and content named with the same word.
translation: Far above every ruler and authority and power and lordship, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one about to come; and he put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fulness of the one who is continually filling the all things with all things.

label: Ephesians 2:2
text:
"Walked" is *peripateō* — literally "to walk around" — worn down by ordinary use into "to conduct one's life, to make one's way." It's locative: the unsaved life is lived entirely inside the sphere of sin, the way a fish lives inside water, never once outside the boundary. The tense is aorist, viewing that whole former life as a single completed unit seen from a distance, not tracked moment by moment. "Course of this world" pairs two ideas that need separating: *kosmos* is humanity's entire system alienated from God across all history, while *aiōn* is the particular spirit or climate of a given age — the zeitgeist, so to speak, of one period within that longer alienation.

"Prince of the power of the air" names Satan with *archōn*, "the first in rank," ruling *exousia*, delegated authority — a term Paul elsewhere applies to demonic forces under Satan's command. "Air" is *aēr*, the thick lower atmosphere close to the ground, distinct from *aithēr*, the clear upper air — Satan's domain is pictured as pressing right up against human life, not remote. "Sons of disobedience" uses the Hebrew idiom in which a person is called "a son of" whatever quality defines him; "disobedience" itself, *apeitheia*, comes from a root meaning "unpersuadable" — not merely someone who disobeys once, but someone constitutionally resistant to being moved.
translation: In which you once walked about, according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the authority of the air, of the spirit now working in the sons of unpersuadableness.

label: Ephesians 2:3
text:
"Had our conversation" is *anastrephō*, an old sense of "conduct oneself" that has nothing to do with talking — Paul is still describing behavior, not speech. "Lusts" is *epithumia*, a strong craving, morally neutral by itself but colored evil here by its source: *sarx*, "flesh," the corrupted human nature. "Fulfilling" is a present participle of *poieō*, "to do" — durative, describing habitual practice rather than a single act, the steady, ongoing performance of what the depraved nature and "mind" (*dianoia*, here plural, meaning the evil thoughts themselves) demanded.

"Were" — "children of wrath" — is imperfect tense, continuous action stretching backward with no starting point in view: not a status entered into at some point but one true from birth onward. "Children" is *teknon*, from the verb "to give birth," stressing the fact of origin rather than legal standing — we didn't drift into this condition, we were born into it, by nature (*phusis*, what is innate, not merely acquired by habit).
translation: Among whom we too all once conducted ourselves in the cravings of our flesh, continually doing the desires of the flesh and of the thoughts, and we were continually children of wrath by nature, even as the rest.

label: Ephesians 2:4–6
text: Paul pivots with a bare *de* — "but" — swinging from the death sentence of the previous verses straight into God's answer. He calls God *plousios* in mercy, "rich," a word that pictures abundant material wealth, not bare sufficiency. The reason is marked with *dia*, "because of": it was his great *agapē*, the deliberate, self-giving love that goes to a cross for the one loved, not mere affection. The verb "made alive," *zōopoieō*, is bound to two others by the same *syn-* prefix — made alive with, raised with, seated with Christ — so that what happened to him in his resurrection and exaltation is now credited to us as if it had happened to us directly. "By grace you have been saved" is a periphrastic construction, a perfect participle plus the present tense of "to be," stacking two ideas at once: the perfect declares the saving act finished with its results fixed, and the present tense of the helping verb declares those results still standing right now. It is a state entered once, and never exited.
translation: But God, being continually rich in mercy, because of his great love with which he loved us, made us — dead as we were in our trespasses — alive together with the Christ (by grace you have been in a saved state, and you remain so), and raised us up together and seated us together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus.

label: Ephesians 2:7
text: The purpose clause looks ahead with a striking phrase — "the ages that are coming upon one another," a stack of future ages rolling in wave after wave, era after era, rather than one uninterrupted stretch of time. What each age keeps displaying is the "surpassing riches of his grace," and the verb "show," *endeiknumi*, stands in the middle voice: God acts for his own interest, putting himself on exhibit through kindness to us. "Kindness," *chrēstotēs*, paired with the preposition *epi*, "upon, toward," frames the saints as the very stage on which this display keeps happening — we are the exhibit, not just the audience.
translation: In order that in the ages continually coming upon one another he might keep on displaying, for his own glory, the surpassing riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.

label: Ephesians 2:8–10
text: "That," in "this is not of yourselves," is neuter — *touto* — while Greek "faith," *pistis*, is feminine, so the pronoun cannot be pointing narrowly back to "faith" as its antecedent; it sweeps up the whole preceding statement, the entire fact of salvation by grace through faith. That whole package is called a gift, sourced in God, not in "works" as its origin. "Workmanship," *poiēma*, comes from the ordinary verb "to make," but the verb used a few words later for God's own creative act is *ktizō*, "to create" — the word reserved for what only God does. Good works were "prepared beforehand," *proetoimazō*, stacking "before" onto "make ready": God laid the works out in advance as the track believers are meant to run, not the ticket that got them onto it. "Walk," *peripateō*, literally "to walk about," is Paul's standing word for the ordering of daily conduct.
translation: For by the grace you have been in a saved state through faith, and this is not from yourselves — it is God's gift — not from works, so that no one may boast; for we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God made ready beforehand, in order that we should be continually walking in them.

label: Ephesians 2:13
text: The contrast turns on two adverbs of distance, "far off" and "near," the standard terms for Gentiles outside the covenant and Jews within it. "Have become near" renders a verb of entering a new state rather than a gradual approach — a decisive, once-for-all shift, and one accomplished specifically "by the blood of Christ," naming the price paid rather than making a vaguer appeal to his life or teaching.
translation: But now, in Christ Jesus, you who once were far off have become near ones by the blood of the Christ.

label: Ephesians 2:14
text: "He himself is our peace" opens with an intensive pronoun, *autos* — not "he too" but "he and no one else." Behind "peace," *eirēnē*, stands the verb "to join," so peace in Paul's vocabulary means fundamentally the joining of what had been split apart, not merely the absence of hostility. What had split Jew and Gentile is pictured architecturally as "the middle wall of the fence" — a boundary marker attached to a barrier, the whole Mosaic system read as a dividing hedge — and Christ's act is described as tearing the wall down, not cutting a gate through it.
translation: For he himself is our peace, the one who made the two groups one, having broken down the dividing wall of the fence.

label: Ephesians 2:15
text: "Abolished," *katargeō*, means to render something inoperative, not to erase it from memory — the law's claims stopped functioning as a dividing wall, put out of commission by Christ's death. The verb behind "make" in "one new man" is not the ordinary "make," *poieō*, but *ktizō*, "create": Paul is not describing a merger of two existing parties into a coalition but the creation of a third thing that did not exist before. And "new," *kainos*, means new in kind rather than new by the calendar, while "man," *anthrōpos*, is the generic human-race word, not *anēr*, "a male individual" — so the entity in view is a new order of humanity, not one group's rebrand.
translation: Having in his flesh rendered inoperative the law of commandments expressed in decrees, so that he might create the two into one new man in himself, making peace.

label: Ephesians 2:16
text: "Reconcile," *apokatallassō*, carries a doubled prefix: *apo*, "back," stacked onto the simple verb "to reconcile." The simple verb, *katallassō*, means to bring together parties who are at odds; the compound suggests not merely a fresh truce between strangers but a restoration to some prior unity that had been lost — Jew, Gentile, and God being returned to how things stood before the rupture, not just patched into a new arrangement.
translation: And that he might reconcile the both, back to their former unity, in one body to God through the cross, having put to death the enmity by it.

label: Ephesians 3:6
text: "Should be," in the underlying Greek, is simply the infinitive "to be" — Paul is stating an already-accomplished fact, not announcing a future goal. Three compounds built on *syn-*, "together with," pile up in a row: *sygklēronoma*, "fellow-heirs"; *syssōma*, "fellow-body-members," belonging jointly to one body; and "fellow-partakers." The manuscripts include the name "Jesus" alongside "Christ" here — without it the sentence could be misread as Gentiles inheriting Israel's own Messianic promises; with "Jesus" attached, the promises in view are specifically those tied to the crucified and risen one, not the covenant promises made to Israel as a nation.
translation: That the Gentiles are fellow-heirs and fellow-body-members and fellow-partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the good news.

label: Ephesians 3:9
text: "Bring to light," *phōtizō*, is built on the noun for light — Paul's task is to shine a light on something previously dim, not to invent it. "Fellowship" translates *oikonomia*, the same household-management word rendered "dispensation" elsewhere; here it names the administrative arrangement itself, the way the mystery is being put into practice, namely Gentile and Jew admitted on equal footing. "World," *aiōn*, means "age" — the mystery was hidden from the very start of the ages, not withheld for merely a generation or two.
translation: And to bring to light what is the administration of the mystery that has been kept hidden away from the ages in God who created all things.

label: Ephesians 3:10
text: "Might be known," *gnōrizō*, and "manifold," *polupoikilos* — literally "much-variegated," a word elsewhere describing richly patterned, many-colored fabric — together picture the church as a display case: God's wisdom, in all its intricate coloring, is being made known to the ranks of angelic rulers and authorities through what happens in the church, not through direct instruction handed to them. The angels are onlookers to redemption, not participants in it — they learn what grace is by watching it worked out among people.
translation: In order that now, through the church, there might be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places the many-colored wisdom of God.

label: Ephesians 3:13
text: "Faint," *egkakeō*, means to lose heart, to give out under pressure — Paul is asking the Ephesians not to let his imprisonment discourage them into giving up. "I desire" is *aiteō* in the middle voice, "to ask for oneself": Paul is not relaying a command but pressing a personal request, that his sufferings be read correctly — as their honor, not his defeat.
translation: For this reason I am asking, on my own behalf, that you not be losing heart at my tribulations for you, which are your glory.

label: Ephesians 3:16
text: The preposition behind "strengthened ... into the inner man" is *eis*, a preposition of motion, "into," not a static "in" — the strengthening is pictured as power in motion, poured toward a destination, with the inward man, the seat of a person's moral and rational self, as the target and receiver rather than the source. That inpouring happens "through the Spirit": the Spirit is the channel of transmission, God's own agent carrying strength from himself into the core of the believer.
translation: That he would grant to you, according to the riches of his glory, to be continually strengthened with power, through his Spirit, into the inward man.

label: Ephesians 3:17–19
text: "Dwell," *katoikeō*, joins "down" to "make one's home" — the sense is settling in permanently, not visiting, and the aorist tense points to a decisive, completed settling rather than a gradual process. "Rooted" and "grounded" are both perfect-tense participles, planted once with the results still holding firm now — one image drawn from a tree's root system, the other from a building's foundation. "Comprehend," *katalambanō*, does not mean intellectual understanding so much as "seize, lay hold of, make one's own" — Paul is praying for something closer to a grip than a grasp. "Know," *ginōskō*, in the next clause shifts registers: it is the verb for knowledge gained by lived experience rather than reasoning, so the prayer moves from a mental laying-hold of Christ's love to that same love being lived and felt. "Passeth" is built on *huperballō*, "to throw beyond": this love outruns the very knowledge just described, so no amount of experiencing it exhausts it.
translation: That the Christ may finally settle down and be at home in your hearts through faith; you having been firmly rooted and grounded in love, so that you may be fully able to lay hold, together with all the saints, of what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know by experience the love of Christ that goes beyond all such knowing — so that you may be filled up to all the fulness of God.

label: Ephesians 4:4–6
text: The passage builds a run of sevenfold repetitions of "one" — body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, "baptism," God — a deliberate drumbeat underlining the unity Paul has just urged. The word usually left untranslated as "baptism," *baptisma*, comes from a verb meaning "to place into" or "immerse." Read for its plain sense rather than transliterated as a technical term, it names the single act by which every believer is placed into the one body — the same placing this letter has already described as being joined to Christ — rather than pointing narrowly to a ceremony.
translation: One body and one Spirit, even as also you were called in one hope of your calling; one Lord, one faith, one placing-into; one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

label: Ephesians 4:7
text: Paul turns from the church's corporate oneness to what belongs to each believer individually. "Grace" here is *charis*, carrying the definite article — the specific enabling grace his readers already know by experience, not *charisma*, the word for the gift itself, but the empowering source behind it. The opening "but" (*de*) is adversative rather than merely transitional: it sets "each one" over against the "all" of the unity just described, so that the oneness of the body never erases the particularity of the member. That grace comes "according to the measure of the gift of Christ" — *metron*, a measured allotment, not an equal share. Christ himself, the giver, sets the size of each portion to fit the calling it serves.
translation: But to each one of us grace was given according to the measure of the gift belonging to the Christ.

label: Ephesians 4:8
text: The "gifts" Christ gives here are *doma*, a plain, general word for something given — not *charisma*, the term for a specific supernatural endowment. Paul is building toward verse 11, where these gifts turn out to be gifted men handed to the church. The verb behind "led captivity captive" is a cognate construction in the Greek, literally "he took captive a captivity" — a Hebraic idiom borrowed from Psalm 68, picturing a conquering king marching his defeated foes home in procession. "Gave" is a simple aorist, a completed, decisive act: the ascension and the distribution of gifts are treated as one accomplished event, not an ongoing process.
translation: Wherefore it says: Having gone up on high, he took captive a host of captives and gave gifts to men.

label: Ephesians 4:13
text: "Till" translates *mechri*, marking a goal line stretching out ahead — "as far as, up to the point where." "Come" is *katantaō*, "to arrive at, to reach" a destination, reinforced by *eis*, "into": the unity of the faith is something the church is still travelling toward, not something already possessed in full. "Knowledge" is *epignōsis*, knowledge intensified — the prefix *epi*- sharpens *gnōsis* into full, precise, firsthand acquaintance rather than secondhand information. "Perfect" is *teleios*, "mature, full-grown" — the deliberate opposite of the "infants" (*nēpioi*) of the very next verse. Growth toward Christ is measured not by an arrival at intellectual consensus but by the church catching up, member by member, to the "stature" — the full measured height — that belongs to him.
translation: Until we all arrive at the oneness of the faith and of the full, precise knowledge of the Son of God, at a mature man, at the measure of the stature of the fullness of the Christ.

label: Ephesians 4:14
text: "Children" is *nēpios* — literally "the non-speaking one," an infant who hasn't yet found words — the deliberate opposite of the "mature man" (*teleios*) of verse 13. "Tossed to and fro" is *kludōnizomai*, a nautical term for being pitched about by wave-swell, applied here to a mind knocked around by every new teaching. "Carried about" is *peripherō*, carried in circles — going nowhere, just churned. "Sleight" is *kubeia*, literally "dice-playing" — the false teacher operates like a cheat at the gaming table, loading the outcome. "Cunning craftiness" is *panourgia*, built from "all" and "work" — a readiness to do absolutely anything to get the result. And "lie in wait to deceive" renders *methodeia*, a deliberate, systematic scheme — the ancestor of our word "method," but here bent entirely toward deception.
translation: In order that we may no longer be infants, wave-tossed and carried around in circles by every wind of teaching, by the dice-player's trickery of men, by craftiness working its system of deceit.

label: Ephesians 4:17
text: "Testify" translates *martureō*, language for a solemn, formal declaration — closer to swearing testimony than casual advice — and Paul adds "in the Lord," making the appeal Christ's own, not merely his. "Walk" is *peripateō*, the standard Greek idiom for a whole pattern of conduct, not a single act. "Vanity" is *mataiotēs* — emptiness, resultlessness, effort that goes nowhere and produces nothing lasting. And "mind" is *nous*, which in Greek carries more than intellect: it's the faculty that judges, discerns, and orients a person morally. A *nous* given over to *mataiotēs* isn't just confused — it has lost the capacity to aim at anything real.
translation: This, therefore, I am saying and solemnly declaring in the Lord: no longer are you to be walking as the Gentiles walk, in the futility of their mind.

label: Ephesians 4:18
text: "Darkened" is a perfect passive participle of *skotoō* — the perfect tense marks an action completed in the past whose effect has settled in and stayed: not a temporary shadow but a permanent condition. "Alienated" is likewise built for a settled state, describing people who have become strangers to "the life of God" — shut out of a relationship, not merely misinformed about one. "Ignorance" is *agnoia*, and Paul locates it "in them" — the fault sits inside the person, not in some accident of upbringing. "Blindness" translates *pōrōsis*, from *pōros*, the word for hardened, callused tissue: the image is of skin gone numb from repeated friction, no longer able to feel what it once felt.
translation: Being those who have been permanently darkened in their understanding, who stand alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the hardening of their heart.

label: Ephesians 4:19
text: "Past feeling" renders *apalgeō*, another perfect participle, describing people who have stopped being able to feel pain or shame — the nerve has gone dead. "Given themselves over" is *paradidōmi*, "to hand over" — the same verb used of Judas handing Jesus to his enemies, or of God "giving over" the rebellious in Romans 1. It's a decisive, aorist act of self-surrender, not a slow drift. "Lasciviousness" is *aselgeia* — a temperament that recognizes no restraint and dares whatever impulse suggests. And the phrase "to work all uncleanness" uses *ergasia*, "a trade, a business": moral corruption pursued the way a man pursues a livelihood, methodically, "with greediness" — *pleonexia*, an appetite that never reaches enough.
translation: Who, being of such a nature as to have become past feeling, handed themselves over to unrestrained wantonness, to the working of every kind of uncleanness in the grip of greediness.

label: Ephesians 4:22–24
text: "Put off" is an aorist infinitive — a decisive, once-for-all action pictured as removing a garment, not a gradual shedding. "Old" is *palaios*, "worn out, used up," not simply "former" — the old self is described as worn through. That old self "is being corrupted" — a present participle, an ongoing decay still underway right up to the moment it's stripped off — "according to the passionate desires of deceit," deceit personified as the force driving the decline. Against that, "renewed" is a present infinitive: a continuous process, not a single event, worked on "the spirit of the mind" — the deep governing disposition, not just opinions. "Put on," like "put off," is aorist — decisive. And "new" is *kainos*, new in kind and quality, not *neos*, merely new in time: this self is a different sort of thing entirely, "created according to God" — patterned directly on him — "in righteousness and holiness of truth," truth personified as the counterweight to the deceit of verse 22.
translation: That you once for all put off, with reference to your former way of life, the old self that is being corrupted through the passionate desires of deceit; and that you are being continually renewed in the spirit of your mind; and that you once for all put on the new self, created according to God in righteousness and holiness that belongs to truth.

label: Ephesians 4:25
text: "Putting away lying" is an aorist participle — a completed act, "having once for all put off the lie," tied straight back to the putting off of the old self two verses earlier. What follows is a present imperative: "be speaking truth," a standing practice, not a single confession. And the reason Paul gives isn't civic decency but anatomy: "we are members belonging to one another" — a lie between believers isn't just a moral failure, it's one organ misinforming another inside a single body.
translation: Therefore, having once for all put off the lie, be continually speaking truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members belonging to one another.

label: Ephesians 4:26
text: Greek has three separate words for anger here, and Paul plays them against each other. *Thumos* is a sudden boil-up of passion, quick to rise and quick to fade — forbidden outright three verses later. *Parorgismos*, "wrath," is anger shot through with irritation and bitterness — also forbidden, in this very verse. *Orgē* is different: a settled, abiding disposition, capable of righteous indignation under the right conditions — and this is the word behind the command "be angry." The verb is a present imperative: keep on holding this settled indignation against what deserves it. The check comes immediately after: "sin not" is also present tense, "stop sinning" — a righteous *orgē* can curdle into something else if left untended, and Paul's deadline for dealing with it is nightfall.
translation: Be continually indignant, and stop sinning. Do not let the sun go down on your irritated, embittered anger.

label: Ephesians 4:27
text: "Neither give place" is a present imperative with a negative — grammar that forbids the continuation of something already happening, not merely a fresh start: "stop giving place," as if the door had already been left ajar. "Place" is *topos*, literally a patch of ground, here "opportunity, room to operate." Unchecked wrath, Paul has just said, hands the devil exactly that — real estate inside a life.
translation: And stop giving the devil room to operate.

label: Ephesians 4:28
text: "Let him steal no more" is built from a present participle plus a present imperative: "the one who is stealing, let him stop stealing" — addressing an ongoing habit, not a single lapse, among people already in the church. The remedy Paul offers isn't merely restraint but redirection: "rather let him labor, working with his own hands" — the same hands once used to take are retrained to produce — "so that he may have something to share with the one who has need." A taker becomes a giver; the cure for theft is generosity.
translation: The one who is stealing, let him steal no longer, but rather let him be laboring, working with his own hands what is good, so that he may have something to be sharing with the one who has need.

label: Ephesians 4:29
text: "Corrupt" is *sapros* — the word for rotten fruit or spoiled food, something decayed past use. Paul pictures speech itself as capable of going bad. "Let it not proceed" is a present imperative: keep such words from ever leaving the mouth, an ongoing vigilance rather than a single filter. The alternative is speech fitted "for building up as the need requires" — practical usefulness, aimed at whoever's actually listening — with the purpose that it "give grace," *charis*, to those who hear: words meant to leave the hearer better off than they found him.
translation: Let no rotten word be proceeding out of your mouth, but only what is good for building up as the need requires, so that it may give grace to those who hear.

label: Ephesians 4:30
text: "Stop grieving" is a present imperative under negation — not a blanket warning against ever grieving the Spirit, but an order to break off something already in motion. The rotten talk and bitterness Paul has just been listing aren't abstract rule-breaking; they're actively wounding a Person who is capable of being grieved. "Whereby," *en hō* — literally "in whom" — locates the seal in the Spirit himself rather than in some separate mark he stamps on. He doesn't merely apply the seal; he is the seal, God's own guarantee stamped onto the believer. And that guarantee runs "to the day of redemption" — not the redemption already accomplished at the cross, but its final installment, the day the purchased body itself is set free.
translation: And stop grieving the Spirit, the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption.

label: Ephesians 4:31
text: Paul stacks near-synonyms to close every exit. *Pikria*, "bitterness," is the resentment that sits and sours rather than passing. *Thumos*, "wrath," is the quick boil-over — anger that flares hot and burns out fast. *Orgē*, "anger," is the settled, simmering kind; note that this is the very word used for the legitimate anger permitted back in 4:26, but here it's forbidden — the same emotion is fine as righteous indignation and poisonous as raw human passion. *Kraugē*, "clamor," is the outward eruption — shouting, brawling, anger gone audible. *Blasphēmia* is slander, speech built to injure. And "put away" is *airō*, which doesn't mean quietly setting something down; it means picking it up bodily and carrying it off. Nothing here gets tolerated in small doses — the command covers every stripe of each vice, root and branch.
translation: Let all bitterness and quick-boiling wrath and simmering anger and brawling and slander be carried off from you, together with all malice.

label: Ephesians 4:32
text: "Be" is *ginomai*, "become" — Paul isn't asking the Ephesians to maintain a state, he's commanding a change of state, and the present tense makes it a continual becoming, not a one-time turn. *Chrēstos*, "kind," is the direct opposite of the harshness just condemned. *Eusplagchnos*, "tenderhearted," is built on the word for inward organs — compassion felt in the gut, not just performed. The real find is "forgiving": Paul doesn't use *aphiēmi*, the word for God legally canceling a debt at the cross, but *charizomai* — to extend a favor, to treat someone graciously regardless of what they've earned. And "in Christ," *en Christō*, is location language, not motive language — it isn't "for Christ's sake" but forgiveness exercised within the sphere Christ creates, the same sphere in which God forgave them.
translation: And keep on becoming kind to one another, tenderhearted, graciously forgiving each other just as God also, in Christ, graciously forgave you.

label: Ephesians 5:5
text: "Ye know" doubles up two different verbs of knowing. *Oida* is absolute, self-evident knowledge — the kind that needs no argument. *Ginōskontes*, from *ginōskō*, is knowledge gained through experience, through having lived it out. Paul isn't offering a new claim; he's reminding them of something they already hold both as settled fact and as something they've watched play out. *Pornos* is the word for one who trades his body for illicit use — a fornicator in the fullest, most physical sense. *Pleonektēs*, "covetous," is someone perpetually reaching for more, particularly what belongs to others. And the sentence ends by redefining that greed theologically: the covetous man is an *eidōlolatrēs*, an idolater — because grasping after more than God gives is functionally worship of something other than God.
translation: For you know this — you know it for certain and you know it from experience — that no fornicator or unclean person or covetous man, who is an idolater, holds an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.

label: Ephesians 5:6
text: "Vain" is *kenos*, "empty, hollow" — words that sound substantial but have nothing inside them, the kind of talk that dresses up self-indulgence as harmless. And "children of disobedience" renders *huios*, "sons" — a Hebrew idiom that doesn't mean people who disobey now and then, but people defined by disobedience as their controlling trait, the way "son of thunder" names a character rather than a single act.
translation: Let no one keep deceiving you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God is coming upon the sons of disobedience.

label: Ephesians 5:7–10
text: "Be" is again *ginomai*, and the command — "stop becoming joint-partakers" — is a present imperative with the negative, meaning this isn't a hedge against a future risk but an order to break off a partnership already forming. "Partakers," *sunmetochos*, doubles the idea of togetherness: *metechō*, "to hold with," plus *sun*, "with," stacked on top of each other. The verb "were" sits in the emphatic position — you *were* darkness, past and finished, which is exactly why becoming it again would be a regression. *Phōs*, "light," names light itself, not a lamp that merely holds it; the Ephesians aren't just illuminated, they're identified as light in the Lord. "Walk," *peripateō*, literally means ordering one's conduct, and the present imperative makes it a standing, habitual practice, not an occasional gesture. "Goodness," *agathōsunē*, is active — doing good, not merely wishing it — and "proving," *dokimazō*, is the language of testing something in order to approve it once it passes.
translation: Stop becoming joint-partakers with them; for you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Be habitually walking as children of light — for the fruit of the light consists in every kind of goodness and righteousness and truth — constantly testing and approving what is well-pleasing to the Lord.

label: Ephesians 5:13
text: "All things" is *ta panta*, "the all things" — the Greek article points back to the specific secret sins just named, not to everything in general. "Made manifest" is *phaneroō*, to drag into visibility what had been hidden, and it's passive: things don't manifest themselves, light does the exposing. The logic runs in a circle worth noticing — whatever gets exposed by light takes on the nature of light itself; exposure isn't just detection, it's a kind of transformation out of the category of darkness altogether.
translation: But all these things, when they are exposed by the light, are made plainly visible, for everything that is being made visible is light.

label: Ephesians 5:14
text: "Give light" translates *epiphauskō*, "to shine upon" — the picture is of dawn breaking over someone still asleep, light arriving from outside rather than something the sleeper produces himself. The quotation stacks sleep and death as parallel pictures of the same condition, and both commands — "wake" and "arise" — are answered not by the sleeper's own effort but by Christ's light falling on him.
translation: Therefore he says: Wake up, you who are sleeping, and rise up from among the dead, and Christ will shine upon you.

label: Ephesians 5:17
text: *Aphrōn*, "unwise," is stronger than careless — it names someone acting without the rational faculty engaged at all, senseless in the moment rather than merely mistaken. "Understanding" is *suniēmi*, built from *syn*, "together," and the verb "to send" — literally putting perception together with the thing perceived, seeing how pieces fit rather than just registering that they exist. And once more *ginomai*, "become," carries a present prohibition: stop an already-moving drift, don't just avoid a future one.
translation: Therefore stop becoming those without reflection, but keep on understanding what the will of the Lord is.

label: Ephesians 5:18–20
text: *Methuskō*, "be drunk," pictures saturation — the same word describes hides soaked through with liquid until pliable. The state in view isn't a single lapse but being permeated all the way through by wine's influence. "Excess," *asōtia*, literally means "un-saving-ness" (*a-* plus *sōzō*, "to save") — a life with no rescuing quality left in it, spending itself toward ruin with nothing to show. Against that, "filled" is *plēroō* in the present imperative passive: not a single completed filling but a repeated, continuous yielding to control, moment by moment. The participles that follow — speaking, singing, making melody, giving thanks — describe what that continual filling looks like in practice, not separate commands but the shape the Spirit-controlled life naturally takes.
translation: And stop being made drunk with wine, in which is dissipation, but keep on being filled by the Spirit — speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord, continually giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God the Father.

label: Ephesians 5:21
text: "Submitting" is *hupotassō*, built from a military root — *tassō* meant arranging troops in battle order under a commanding officer, and the prefix *hupo* adds "under." In the middle voice, as it is here, the sense is self-chosen: not a rank imposed from outside but a position a person places himself into. The present participle keeps it a standing posture rather than a single decision made once and left behind.
translation: Continually placing yourselves in submission to one another in the fear of Christ.

label: Ephesians 5:24
text: The connecting word is *alla*, the strongest adversative in Greek — "but," not "therefore." That matters: the verse isn't drawing a conclusion from what precedes, it's setting up a contrast. Christ is Savior of the body in a way no husband is; that difference stands. But the difference doesn't cancel the pattern — *hupotassō* again, middle voice, a self-given submission — because the point of the analogy was never that husbands equal Christ in every respect, only that the church's relation to Christ supplies the shape wives are to follow toward their husbands.
translation: But just as the church submits itself to Christ, so also let the wives submit themselves to their husbands in everything.

label: Ephesians 5:25–27
text: The verb for the husband's love is *agapaō* — the self-giving love God is, the love shown at the cross, set apart from the other loves a husband might also feel (passion, fond affection, simple liking) by its willingness to spend itself for another's good rather than seek its own. "Sanctify," *hagiazō*, means setting apart for sacred use, and "cleansing" rides alongside it as the means by which that setting-apart happens. The washing itself, *loutron*, is a bath — an act, not just a substance — and "by the word," *en hrēmati*, is locative: the cleansing happens within the sphere the word creates, the word doing the purifying work water only pictures. The purpose clause that follows — "that he might present the church to himself" — uses a decisive, one-time verb: a future, single moment of presentation, not an ongoing process, the wedding day toward which all the cleansing has been aimed. "Without blemish," *amōmos*, is sacrificial language — the term for an animal offered with no defect, faultless by inspection.
translation: Husbands, keep on loving your wives just as Christ also loved the church and gave himself up on its behalf, so that he might sanctify it, cleansing it by the washing of water in the sphere of the word, so that he might present the church to himself in glory, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that it might be holy and without blemish.

label: Ephesians 5:28–30
text: Paul's hōs (ὡς, "as") in "love their wives as their own bodies" carries qualitative force — not "in a similar way," but "as being." The logic runs from the one-flesh union: the wife is, in a very real sense, an extension of the husband's own self, so love for her is nature, not mere duty. Verse 30 opens in the Greek with melē (μέλη, "members") thrown forward for emphasis — "Members we are of his body" — underscoring that believers are not merely associated with Christ but organically part of him. The clause "of his flesh and of his bones" is missing from the earliest manuscripts and is bracketed by most modern editors as a later addition drawn from Genesis 2:23.
translation: In this way also, husbands ought to be loving their wives as being their own bodies. The one continually loving his own wife is loving himself, for no one has ever yet hated his own flesh, but is continually nourishing and cherishing it, even as the Christ does the church, because members are we of his body.

label: Ephesians 5:31
text: "Leave" translates kataleípō (καταλείπω), "to leave behind, depart from" — a decisive break from the family of origin. "Joined" is proskollaō (προσκολλάω), literally "to glue onto"; the prefixed preposition intensifies the plain verb into an image of adhesive, permanent bonding. And "one flesh" carries the preposition eis (εἰς, "into") in the Greek — not a static fact declared but a union arrived at: the two do not simply find themselves one flesh, they become it.
translation: Because of this, a man shall leave behind his father and his mother and shall be glued fast to his wife, and the two shall come to be one flesh.

label: Ephesians 6:4
text: "Provoke" translates parorgízō (παροργίζω), "to rouse to wrath, exasperate" — the command targets a specific parental failure, needling children into resentment through harshness or favoritism. "Bring up" is ektrephō (ἐκτρέφω), the same root used of feeding an infant, now extended to cover the whole process of nurturing a child to maturity. The pairing that follows separates two methods of that nurture: paideia (παιδεία) is training by action — correction, discipline, structured formation — while nouthēsia (νουθεσία) is training by word, the spoken warning that addresses the mind directly.
translation: And you fathers, stop provoking your children to wrath, but keep on rearing them in the discipline and admonition of the Lord.

label: Ephesians 6:5–8
text: Paul calls these believers douloi (δοῦλοι), "slaves" — real chattel slaves with pagan owners, not household employees in any modern sense. He labels their owners kurios (κύριος, "lord, master") rather than the harsher despotēs used elsewhere in the New Testament, then qualifies it "according to the flesh" — masters only in the earthly sphere, since the slave's true Kurios is in heaven. "Fear and trembling" is Paul's stock phrase, used elsewhere of himself and of the Corinthians and Philippians, for earnest, careful diligence rather than literal dread. "Singleness of heart" is undivided sincerity, set against eye-service — service rendered only under the master's watching eye, calculated to win favor rather than flowing from real goodwill. "Heart" here is actually psuchē (ψυχή), "soul": the service is to rise from the whole inner self, done as if rendered to Christ, with reward tracking the deed and not the social rank of the one who did it.
translation: Slaves, keep on obeying those who are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as to Christ; not by way of eye-service, as men-pleasers, but as slaves of Christ, doing the will of God from the soul; rendering service with good will, as to the Lord and not to men, knowing that whatever good each one does, this he will receive back from the Lord, whether he is slave or free.

label: Ephesians 6:9
text: The command to masters mirrors the one just given to slaves — "do the same things" does not mean serving in return, but applying the identical Christian standard. "Forbearing" is aniēmi (ἀνίημι), "to let go, give up," aimed at "the threatening" — the definite article points to a habitual, expected practice, the standing threat masters used to keep order. The reasoning is theological: master and slave answer to the same Kurios in heaven, so there can be no prosōpolēmpsia (προσωπολημψία) — literally "receiving of face," judging by outward rank instead of the person's actual worth.
translation: And masters, keep on doing the same things toward them, giving up your threatening, knowing that both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no receiving of a face with him.

label: Ephesians 6:10
text: "Be strong" renders a passive verb, endunamoō (ἐνδυναμόω) — not a summons to self-generated grit but an instruction to be strengthened, to receive strength poured in from outside, the way one puts on a garment. "Power" (kratos, κράτος) is strength as displayed and exercised, while "might" (ischus, ἰσχύς) is the underlying capacity, strength held in reserve. Paul stacks both to describe not just God's raw resource of power but its active, effectual working on the believer's behalf.
translation: Finally, be continually strengthened in the Lord and in the active working of his might.

label: Ephesians 6:11
text: "Put on" is enduō (ἐνδύω), "to clothe oneself with." The "whole armor" is panoplia (πανοπλία) — pas (πᾶς, "all") plus hoplon (ὅπλον, "weapon") — a soldier's complete equipment, not any one piece of it. The genitive "of God" marks source, and the real weight falls on the completeness of the set: armor supplied by God but taken up only in part still leaves gaps. "Wiles" translates methodeia (μεθοδεία), built from a verb meaning "to follow a fixed method or system" — not a random assault but calculated, systematic stratagem. "Stand" is soldier's language for holding one's ground under attack, the opposite of retreat.
translation: Put on the full armor of God, so that you may be able to stand your ground against the calculated stratagems of the devil.

label: Ephesians 6:12
text: "Wrestle" is palē (πάλη), a specific athletic term for the grappling contest in which two opponents fight to pin one another — close, personal, all-or-nothing combat, a shift from the massed-formation soldier imagery that frames the rest of the passage. Kosmokratōr (κοσμοκράτωρ, "world-ruler") is a compound of kosmos ("world, order") and krateō ("to hold power") — naming spirit-beings whose reach is cosmic, not petty local troublemakers. "Heavenly places" here is the lower atmosphere ringing the earth, the domain Paul elsewhere assigns to Satan's forces, not the highest heaven where God dwells.
translation: Because our wrestling is not against blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

label: Ephesians 6:13
text: "Take up" is analambanō (ἀναλαμβάνω) in the aorist imperative — a decisive, once-for-all command rather than an ongoing process: put the armor on completely, now, and keep it on. "Withstand" is anthístēmi (ἀνθίστημι), "to stand against, resist" — military language for holding a line under direct assault. The definite article before "day" singles out one particular day of testing, not days in general. "Done" translates katergazomai (κατεργάζομαι), "to work out to completion" — not merely surviving the assault but fighting it through to the end.
translation: Therefore, take up the full armor of God at once, so that you will be able to resist in the evil day, and, having fought everything through to the end, to stand.

label: Ephesians 6:14–17
text: The verbs "having girded," "having put on," "having shod" are middle voice, not passive — the armor does not fall on the believer automatically; each piece is his own to take up. The girdle is "truth," and its function is structural, not ornamental: it cinches everything else into place and frees the legs for movement. "Righteousness" as breastplate is the ongoing, lived integrity of the believer's conduct guarding the heart — not the once-for-all righteousness credited at conversion. "Preparation" (hetoimazō, ἑτοιμάζω) carried in classical usage the sense of a firm, settled foundation — the gospel of peace gives solid footing, not merely readiness to move. The shield, thureos (θυρεός), is the large, oblong, door-shaped shield covering the whole body — the word is built on thura, "door" — designed to catch and quench arrows dipped in pitch and set alight. The sword, machaira (μάχαιρα), is the short weapon for close combat, and it is identified with rhēma (ῥῆμα) — not Scripture as an abstract whole but the specific word of God spoken and applied in the moment of need.
translation: Stand, therefore, having girded your loins with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, and having shod your feet with the firm-footing readiness that comes from the good news of peace; in addition to all these, having taken up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the flaming arrows of the evil one; and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the spoken word of God.

label: Ephesians 6:18
text: "Always" is en panti kairō (ἐν παντὶ καιρῷ), "at every season" — not a vague general disposition but prayer fitted to each occasion as it arises. Paul stacks proseuchē (προσευχή), prayer in general, with deēsis (δέησις), a specific plea for a particular need. "Watching" is agrupneō (ἀγρυπνέω), literally "being sleepless" — deliberate, wide-awake vigilance, the opposite of drifting into dullness. "Perseverance" is proskarteréō (προσκαρτερέω), "to give unremitting, continuous attention" — sustained effort, not a single burst. Turning the request toward himself, Paul asks for logos (λόγος), "utterance" — a specific word supplied for the moment — spoken with parrēsia (παρρησία), literally "all-speech," the freedom to say the whole thing without holding back, fitting for a man making his case in chains.
translation: Praying at every season, with every prayer and supplication, in the Spirit, and staying sleeplessly watchful toward this very thing with all unremitting attention and supplication for all the saints; and on my behalf, that utterance may be given me in the opening of my mouth, to make known with full freedom of speech the mystery of the good news.

label: Ephesians 6:21–24
text: Paul sends Tychicus not merely as a messenger but explicitly "for this very purpose" — a purpose clause naming the reason: so the Ephesians will know Paul's circumstances, and so Tychicus can parakaleō (παρακαλέω) their hearts, a verb meaning to comfort and strengthen by coming alongside. The closing benediction stacks three words with precision — eirēnē (εἰρήνη, "peace"), agapē (ἀγάπη, "love"), and pistis (πίστις, "faith") — asked from Father and Son together as a single source. The letter's final phrase, "in sincerity," translates en aphtharsia (ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ), literally "in incorruption" — a love for Christ that does not decay, spoil, or wear thin with time.
translation: But in order that you also may know my circumstances, what I am doing, Tychicus, the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord, will make everything known to you, whom I sent to you for this very purpose, that you may know our circumstances and that he may comfort your hearts. Peace to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all those who are loving our Lord Jesus Christ with a love that does not decay.
